title: Mock 7 · Tough II
blurb: Final dress rehearsal: option-strategy and bond-hedge caselets, NOT/multi-statement items and heavier numericals.

questions.q: What are the break-even points of Kabir's long straddle?
questions.explanation: Long straddle BEPs = strike ± total premium.
hints: Wrong — uses only the call premium.
Wrong — uses only the put premium.
Wrong — those are the strangle's break-evens (2,100 + 55 and 1,900 − 55).
Correct — total premium = 70 + 55 = 125; BEPs = 2,000 ± 125.
questions.case: XYZ Ltd trades at ₹2,000 a day before its quarterly results. Near-month option premiums (lot size 250): 2,000 call ₹70; 2,000 put ₹55; 2,100 call ₹30; 1,900 put ₹25. Trader Kabir expects a sharp move but is unsure of direction. He compares a long straddle at the 2,000 strike with a long strangle using the 2,100 call and the 1,900 put. All options are European and held to expiry; ignore costs.

questions.q: If XYZ closes at ₹2,180 on expiry, what is Kabir's profit per lot on the long strangle?
questions.explanation: Long strangle: profit = payoff of ITM leg − total premium; upper BEP = 2,100 + 55 = 2,155.
hints: Wrong — that ignores the premium paid.
Correct — call payoff 2,180 − 2,100 = 80; less total premium 30 + 25 = 55 ⇒ 25 × 250 = ₹6,250.
Wrong — that is the total premium paid per lot.
Wrong — the strangle is profitable above 2,155.

Trader Kabir expects a sharp move but is unsure of direction. He compares a long straddle at the 2,000 strike with a long strangle using the 2,100 call and the 1,900 put. All options are European and held to expiry; ignore costs.

questions.q: If XYZ closes exactly at ₹2,000 on expiry, which statement is correct?
options: The straddle loses ₹13,750 and the strangle ₹31,250 per lot
The straddle loses its maximum ₹31,250 per lot, while the strangle loses ₹13,750 per lot
The straddle earns the full premium of ₹31,250
questions.explanation: Maximum loss of a long straddle is at the strike; a strangle costs less, so its maximum loss is smaller but it needs a bigger move to profit.
hints: Wrong — neither breaks even at 2,000.
Wrong — the figures are swapped.
Correct — at the strike both straddle legs expire worthless (125 × 250); both strangle legs are OTM too (55 × 250).
Wrong — a LONG straddle pays the premium; it does not earn it.

Trader Kabir expects a sharp move but is unsure of direction. He compares a long straddle at the 2,000 strike with a long strangle using the 2,100 call and the 1,900 put. questions.q: To hedge, what should the bank do in the futures market?
options: Sell 500 lots of the October bond futures
Buy 500 lots of the October bond futures
Sell 50 lots of the October bond futures
Buy 500 lots of overnight MIBOR futures at the bond yield
questions.explanation: Holder of a bond is long bonds / short rates; a short hedge sells bond futures (lots = FV ÷ ₹2 lakh for a same-bond hedge).
hints: Correct — ₹10 crore ÷ ₹2 lakh = 500 lots, and a short futures position gains if yields rise.
Wrong — buying would add to the rate risk.
Wrong — the lot is ₹2 lakh FV, so 500 lots are needed.
Wrong — MIBOR futures hedge short-term rates, not this bond's price.
questions.case: On 1 September, a co-operative bank holds 6.80% GS 2035 with a face value of ₹10 crore at a clean price of ₹99.00. It fears yields will rise after the October policy review but does not want to sell the bond. Cash-settled single-bond futures on the same G-sec, expiring on the last Thursday of October, trade at ₹98.90 (lot: face value ₹2 lakh). On the October expiry date both the bond and the futures settle at ₹97.40. Ignore accrued interest, margins and costs.

questions.q: What is the gain on the bank's futures position at expiry?
questions.explanation: IRF P&L = price change × 2,000 × lots.
hints: Wrong — that uses the cash price of 99.00.
Wrong — that uses 50 lots.
Wrong — that halves the lot.
questions.case: On 1 September, a co-operative bank holds 6.80% GS 2035 with a face value of ₹10 crore at a clean price of ₹99.00. It fears yields will rise after the October policy review but does not want to sell the bond. Cash-settled single-bond futures on the same G-sec, expiring on the last Thursday of October, trade at ₹98.90 (lot: face value ₹2 lakh). On the October expiry date both the bond and the futures settle at ₹97.40. Ignore accrued interest, margins and costs.

questions.q: Ignoring accrued interest, what is the bank's net result from the bond and the hedge together, and why?
options: A net loss of about ₹1,00,000, because the hedge locked the futures price of ₹98.90 rather than the spot price of ₹99.00
Zero, because the hedge is perfect
A net loss of ₹16,00,000, because cash-settled futures pay nothing
questions.explanation: A hedge locks in roughly the futures price; basis (spot − futures) explains the residual. In practice the bank also earns accrued interest on the bond.
hints: Correct — bond value falls (99.00 − 97.40) × ₹10 lakh per rupee = ₹16,00,000; futures gain ₹15,00,000; the initial basis of ₹0.10 per bond remains.
Wrong — the initial basis creates a small difference.
Wrong — that ignores the loss on the bond.
Wrong — cash-settled futures do pay the P&L in cash.

questions.q: A 30-year-old software engineer with high income, no dependants and a 20-year horizon says she 'cannot sleep' if her portfolio falls 5%. How should her risk profile be described?
options: Low risk capacity and high risk appetite
High risk capacity and high risk appetite
High risk capacity but low risk appetite (tolerance)
Low risk capacity and low risk appetite
questions.explanation: Risk profiling considers both capacity (ability) and appetite/tolerance (willingness); advice should respect the lower of the two.
hints: Wrong — her capacity is high, not low.
Wrong — her stated discomfort shows low appetite.
Correct — her finances can bear risk, but her willingness to bear it is low.
Wrong — her capacity is high.

questions.q: Consider: I. In an interval scheme, the transaction period must be at least 2 working days. II. The interval period must be at least 15 days. III. MF Lite is a relaxed regime available to all categories of active schemes. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: Interval scheme: transaction period ≥ 2 working days; interval period ≥ 15 days. MF Lite covers only passive schemes (index funds, ETFs, FoFs).
hints: Wrong — III is false.
Wrong — III is false and I is true.
Wrong — III is false and II is true.
Correct — MF Lite applies only to passive schemes, so III is false.

questions.q: In which SIF strategy, if the fund manager goes short on a sector, must all stocks of that sector be held as short positions?
questions.explanation: Sector Rotation Long-Short: min 80% equity, max 4 sectors, shorts at sector level, ≤ 25% unhedged short.
hints: Wrong — Equity Long-Short operates at stock level.
Wrong — Ex-Top 100 operates at stock level.
Wrong — Active Asset Allocator is a multi-asset hybrid strategy.
Correct — Sector Rotation operates at sector level, not stock level.

questions.q: An AMC that already runs mutual fund schemes wants to launch an SIF. According to the workbook, it:
options: Can launch automatically under its existing MF registration with no further conditions
Must fulfil additional requirements and eligibility criteria specified by SEBI
Must register a separate AMC under SEBI (PMS) Regulations
questions.explanation: The AMCs desirous of launching an SIF shall fulfil the additional requirements and eligibility criteria specified by SEBI.
hints: Wrong — additional criteria apply.
Correct — AMCs desirous of launching SIF shall meet additional SEBI eligibility criteria.
Wrong — SIF is under the MF Regulations, not PMS.
Wrong — RBI does not approve SIF launches.

questions.q: Which of the following statements on investment restrictions under the SEBI MF Regulations 2026 is NOT correct?
options: A fund of funds scheme may invest in another fund of funds scheme
A scheme may invest in another scheme of the same or another MF without charging fees, subject to limits
Mutual funds may engage in short selling in accordance with SEBI's short selling and securities lending framework
Pending deployment, scheme funds may be parked in short-term deposits of scheduled commercial banks
questions.explanation: Sixth Schedule: no scheme may invest in a FoF; FoFs invest only in MF schemes (plus liquidity needs).
hints: Correct — this is incorrect — a FoF shall not invest in any other FoF, and no scheme may invest in a FoF.
Wrong — this is a correct provision.
Wrong — this is correct.
Wrong — this is correct.

questions.q: If the risk level of an SIF investment strategy changes, how must it be communicated?
options: Only at the next annual report
Through a notice-cum-addendum and by email or SMS to unitholders of that strategy
No communication is needed as the band is reviewed annually
questions.explanation: Risk-Band: set at NFO, evaluated monthly; changes communicated via notice-cum-addendum and email/SMS; monthly and annual disclosures.
hints: Wrong — communication must be prompt, not annual.
Wrong — AMFI disclosure is in addition, not a substitute.
Correct — changes require a notice-cum-addendum and email/SMS to affected unitholders.
Wrong — the band is evaluated monthly and changes must be communicated.

questions.q: For which of the following distributors must AMCs disclose commission paid and carry out additional due diligence? I. Commission of ₹60 lakh p.a. from a single AMC. II. Presence in 15 locations with ₹40 crore non-institutional AUM. III. Industry-wide commission of ₹1.2 crore p.a.
questions.explanation: Triggers (any one): >20 locations; >₹100 crore non-institutional AUM; >₹1 crore commission p.a. industry-wide; >₹50 lakh from a single AMC.
hints: Wrong — II does not qualify.
Correct — I exceeds ₹50 lakh from one AMC; III exceeds ₹1 crore industry-wide; II fails both the 20-location and ₹100 crore tests.
Wrong — II does not qualify; I and III do.
Wrong — II does not qualify and I does.

questions.q: What is the TER ceiling for a close-ended debt scheme?
questions.explanation: Close-ended and interval schemes: equity-oriented 1.00%; others 0.80%.
hints: Wrong — 1.00% is the cap for close-ended equity-oriented schemes.
Wrong — 1.85% is the open-ended non-equity first slab.
Correct — close-ended/interval schemes other than equity-oriented are capped at 0.80%.
Wrong — 0.90% is the index fund/ETF cap.

questions.q: An investor redeems units of a hybrid fund that holds 50% in domestic equity after 30 months (redeemed after 23 July 2024). How are the gains taxed?
options: At the investor's slab rate irrespective of holding period
As long-term gains at 12.5% with a ₹1.25 lakh exemption, like equity funds
questions.explanation: Tax table: equity-oriented 20%/12.5% (12 months, ₹1.25 lakh exemption); hybrid 35–65% equity: STCG slab, LTCG 12.5% after 24 months; debt-oriented: slab.
hints: Correct — hybrids with 35–65% equity are LTCG after 24 months at 12.5%.
Wrong — 20% STCG applies to equity-oriented funds held ≤12 months.
Wrong — slab-only treatment applies to funds with >65% debt.
Wrong — the ₹1.25 lakh exemption is for equity-oriented funds.

questions.q: An SIF Equity Long-Short strategy proposes daily subscriptions and fortnightly redemptions. Is this permissible?
options: No — subscription and redemption frequencies must match
No — equity SIF strategies must allow daily redemptions
Yes — but only if it is converted to a close-ended scheme
Yes — SIF frequencies may differ, and equity strategies may allow redemption daily or at any lesser frequency
questions.explanation: SIF exception: subscription and redemption frequencies can differ; equity strategy redemptions daily or lesser frequency.
hints: Wrong — matching frequencies is required only for regular MF schemes.
Wrong — 'daily or any lesser frequency' permits fortnightly.
Wrong — no conversion is required.
Correct — SIF can have distinct frequencies; equity SIF redemptions can be daily or less frequent.

questions.q: ₹50,000 invested in a growth fund became ₹72,000 in exactly 3 years. What is the CAGR?
questions.explanation: CAGR = (LV/IV)^(1/n) − 1.
hints: Wrong — that is the simple return ÷ 3.
Wrong — that is the absolute return.
Wrong — not supported by the formula.

questions.q: Which investor is LEAST suitable for an SIF Debt Long-Short strategy?
options: A retiree with ₹12 lakh who needs the money available on any day for medical emergencies
An HNI with ₹50 lakh surplus and a 3-year horizon comfortable with weekly liquidity
A business owner investing ₹15 lakh who understands derivative-based shorting
A family office allocating ₹1 crore across SIF strategies
questions.explanation: Suitability: SIF needs ₹10 lakh+, higher risk appetite, and acceptance of interval/limited liquidity.
hints: Correct — debt SIFs are interval schemes with at most weekly redemptions and carry short-position risk — unsuitable for emergency money.
Wrong — meets threshold, horizon and liquidity comfort.
Wrong — meets threshold and understands the product.
Wrong — meets threshold and diversifies across strategies.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the Ind AS 109 criteria for a financial derivative?
options: Its value is linked to the value of an underlying
It must be traded on a recognised stock exchange
It is settled on a future date
It requires no full cash outlay on the trade date
questions.explanation: Ind AS 109: value linked to underlying; settlement on a future date; no full cash outlay on trade date.
hints: Wrong — this is a criterion.
Correct — this is not an Ind AS 109 criterion; OTC derivatives also qualify.
Wrong — this is a criterion.
Wrong — this is a criterion (it gives leverage).

questions.q: Best bid is ₹100.30. Sell orders: 500 shares at ₹100.50, 1,000 at ₹100.60, 1,500 at ₹100.80. What is the impact cost of buying 1,200 shares?
questions.explanation: Impact cost = (actual execution price − ideal price) ÷ ideal price × 100; ideal = mid of best bid and ask.
hints: Wrong — that measures from the best bid (100.30) instead of the ideal price.
Wrong — that measures from the best offer (100.50) instead of the ideal price.
Wrong — that assumes all 1,200 shares fill at ₹100.60.

questions.q: A stock trades at ₹800 and its 1-month futures at ₹812 (lot 500). Financing costs 9% p.a. (simple). Ignoring other costs, the locked-in cash-and-carry arbitrage profit per lot is:
questions.explanation: Futures above fair value ⇒ buy spot, sell futures; profit = (futures − fair price) × lot.
hints: Wrong — that ignores the financing cost.
Wrong — not supported by the data.
Wrong — not supported by the data.

questions.q: Consider SEBI's lot size rules: I. Index derivative lots are a multiple of 5 with a minimum of 10. II. Stock derivative lots are a multiple of 25 with a minimum of 50. III. Lot sizes are reviewed every 3 months with one week's notice. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: Lot size review: once in 6 months based on last one month's average closing price; at least 2 weeks' advance notice.
hints: Wrong — III is incorrect.
Correct — reviews are every 6 months with at least 2 weeks' notice, so III is wrong.
Wrong — III is incorrect and I is correct.
Wrong — III is incorrect and II is correct.

questions.q: What is the sign of delta for a short (written) put position?
questions.explanation: Delta: long call 0 to +1; short call 0 to −1; long put 0 to −1; short put 0 to +1.
hints: Wrong — negative delta is for a long put or short call.
Wrong — delta is zero only for deep OTM options near expiry.
Wrong — option deltas lie between −1 and +1.
Correct — a long put has negative delta, so a short put has positive delta — it gains when the underlying rises.

questions.q: If interest rates rise with all other factors unchanged, option premiums will typically:
options: Rise for both calls and puts
Fall for calls and rise for puts
Rise for calls and fall for puts
Fall for both calls and puts
questions.explanation: Interest rate ↑ ⇒ call ↑, put ↓ (rho: call +, put −).
hints: Wrong — only volatility and time move both the same way.
Wrong — reversed.
Correct — calls have positive rho; puts negative rho.
Wrong — not the effect described in the workbook.

questions.q: An investor owns a stock at ₹1,590, sells a 1,600 call for ₹10 and buys a 1,580 put for ₹7. This position is a:
questions.explanation: Collar extends a covered call by buying an OTM put to floor the downside; it also lowers the maximum profit.
hints: Correct — long stock + short OTM call + long OTM put = collar.
Wrong — a butterfly uses three strikes of the same option type.
Wrong — a protective put has no short call.
Wrong — a short strangle sells both options.

questions.q: The current-month Nifty futures trade at 25,000 and the next-month at 25,180. What is the roll cost?
questions.explanation: Roll cost = (Next series price − Current series price) ÷ Current series price × 100.
hints: Wrong — that divides by 100,000.
Wrong — that misplaces the decimal.
Wrong — that misplaces the decimal.

questions.q: For a bond trading at a premium to par, the correct relationship is:
questions.explanation: Par: CR = CY = YTM; discount: CR < CY < YTM; premium: CR > CY > YTM.
hints: Wrong — that describes a discount bond.
Wrong — that describes a par bond.
Wrong — not a valid ordering.
Correct — premium bonds pay a coupon above the market yield.

questions.q: Derivatives whose underlying is a theoretical bond (not a physically available bond) with fixed maturity and coupon are called:
questions.explanation: IRD underlyings: interest rates, notional bonds, single bonds, bond indices.
hints: Wrong — single bond futures reference a specific G-sec.
Wrong — money market futures reference short-term rates such as MIBOR.
Correct — a notional bond's price is inferred from a basket of deliverable bonds.
Wrong — index futures reference an index of bonds.

questions.q: The 6-month spot rate is 6.00% and the 1-year spot rate is 6.40%, both with semi-annual compounding. The 6-month rate, 6 months forward (annualised, semi-annual compounding), is about:
questions.explanation: Forward rate from spot rates: (1 + S1/2)^(2×1) = (1 + S0.5/2)^(2×0.5) × (1 + F/2).
hints: Wrong — that is the simple average.
Wrong — that is the 1-year spot rate.
Wrong — not supported by the formula.

questions.q: An investor buys one lot of a GOI bond call option with a strike of ₹100.25 at a premium of ₹0.15. The bond settles at ₹100.75 on expiry. What is the net profit for the lot?
questions.explanation: Long call P&L = max(S − X, 0) − premium per ₹100 FV × 2,000 bonds.
hints: Wrong — that ignores the premium.
Wrong — that uses the premium as the gain.
Wrong — that halves the payoff.
